transcript.content: It's just gone five past four. It's the Ricky Gervais Show. That's Steve just doing the microphone, putting his headphones on, making-
Sorry, I- you just didn't give me much time to prepare myself. Sorry.
Um, I think that's working. My headphones are not quite working. Hang on.
Well, not only haven't- not prepared for the show-
Yeah, OK. I thought maybe people could phone in and give us some subjects to uh, uh, talk about.

Or they can fax in 0171 580 1234, and they could get, like, a discussion going, like, “What do you think of that Tour de France nonsense?” And we could sort of— no, not that. Um, what do you think about, uh... Well, you know, it’s their idea, innit?
Quickly, I mean really, seriously just get on the phone now.
This is my record of the week.

It's quite interesting. I think it's quite interesting, Rick, because, um, you know, it's a very sensitive song, a very beautiful song, and I think it betrays something about you, about the inner Ricky.
Which I don't think uh, we've ever sort of really tapped into before.
No, but I mean, I've got something exciting for you as well.
’Cause maybe you, you know, you can find love too. ’Cause Petru’s sent in, uh, a piece of paper here from, uh— see there? From Mixmag.
But it’s the, uh, personal ads. Oh no, it’s not, it’s an ad. It’s Select. That’s an advert for Mixmag.
Whatever, Rick. It doesn't really matter, does it?
Realism, it makes all the difference.
So they don’t think I’m just making it up.
Right. Lonely, depressed, bi-girl needs someone of any age to understand. Right? Any age. Right, yeah. Well, that fits, you know, your any age.
Well, don't count your chickens. Don't count your chickens.
Now, I know what you're thinking.
No, give- no, give it to me now.

I know what she said. I know I know what you're thinking. It's just any age which you fall into nicely. Um, Ugly freaks preferred, so you're at the top of the list, and anyone accepted. See, I, but I don't think she realises quite what you look like, because you're not in her framework.
Do you know what I mean? So I I still think you might be disappointed.
This’ll work. Let me see this. “Lonely depressed bi girl.”
What does that mean, though? Bi girl. What is that?
Yeah. Again, I think she means...
Sexuality of any human. Do you know what I mean?
Well, all I'm saying, bisexual, Gervais. Do you know what I mean? Am I right?
Hey! Three! You know? Eh? Three people?
You, a bisexual and an amphibian.
But you won't be one of them.
It's not going to happen, is it?
Twenty-five past four. Ricky Gervais Show. I’m Ricky Gervais.
Gervais, um, I know we haven't got much in the show today. We've not really thought of anything to talk about. Why did you just give a time check then?
But, like, why? D’you know what I mean? ’Cause the music—
It’s sunny out as well, innit?

And you mentioned it’s twenty-five past four. Um, we’d never do time checks. How is that useful? What are you expecting? Someone’s looking at it, they’re gonna think, “Twenty-five past four? Christ, I should be at my mum’s house!”
“They haven’t played any good records. They’re quite— they’re interesting, but thank God he told me what it was. I’ve got to take that bun out the oven.”
But you don't want to tell...
Or they probably just realised something good's starting on telly.
Well, exactly, that’s what I was gonna say. Don’t say it’s twenty-five past four because, you know, I dunno, maybe the Antiques Roadshow’s on.
No, BBC always start things at twenty-five past, don’t they?
Well, You're a fool, that's what I'm saying. There's no reason for time checks.
Why do they do that? Why— why do they do that, and not on the hour like ITV? You know where you are with ITV. BBC, ten past, quarter past.
Well, I'll tell you what I'm gonna do. I'm gonna uh, quickly go to an ad break, which is good.
That, That keeps people pretty fixed.
Oh yeah, yeah, they’ll be desperate.
They’ll be listening to those ads.
But I’ll do a little trail. Watch this. Uh, but after that, if you can, uh, hold out for forty seconds, we’ve got the new one from the Manic Street Preachers. You gotta be happy with that.
Um, I watched Team Knight Rider yesterday.
It’s a new— new sort of thing. Must be made ten years later. And it’s, uh, instead of just the one Knight Rider car, it’s a team of ’em. A fleet of ’em, Gervais.
Team, I think you said teen.
Yeah, when he was little, he had spots and he was a little bit embarrassed.
On like a little, uh, little sort of scooter.
Yeah. And you go up to girls and go, “Hello! Uh, d’you wanna, uh... d’you wanna... oh.” Yeah. Teen Knight Rider.
And Kit goes, what are you doing? Nothing.
“I was just— no, no, I was... I got [unclear] caught in the flies!”
He's like- KITT's there sort of explaining how to shave.
You dirty little... Now that has really gummed up my CD player now.
Oh, we'd better stop it there, shall we?
I tell you, if we get off to talking about telly programmes, Gervais, we’ll be here all night.
Yeah, well, it’s about twenty-five past four now.
Uh, but listen, Gervais, you know I’ve always said that, um, you know when a party’s going bad?
When you end up in the kitchen, uh, talking about old kids' TV shows.
And do you remember Swizzlers? Oh, yeah, yeah. And Flying Saucers, yes, we remember Flying Saucers.
And Batwing Jumpers. Ha, ha, ha, ha. And everyone starts laughing. Obviously.
Do you not remember Batwing Jumpers?
Grotbags. Grotbags. What was that? That was, That was.
Talk about gay subtext. Pink Windmill.
So I take it with the fact that we're talking about it. We're in the kitchen at a bad party.
We're in the kitchen at a bad party.
We've got nothing to talk about.
You know, usually we say, oh, we've got nothing, we've got a couple of things and we get out. We've really got nothing, have we?
What about that Teen Knight Rider? We were going somewhere. There— there must be something.
Oh, Teen Knight Rider, yeah. Hilarious. Imagine it.
What was it? [Sings the Knight Rider theme.]
"Michael, it's time for school." "Oh, come on, I've got bellyache." "Well, you're well enough to do that." "I have to do that! I have to get rid of my poison!" Um...
Well, uh, yeah, no, but teen... I wasn't talking about teen Knight Rider.
No, sorry, Team Knight Rider. You actually— you were actually gonna tell an anecdote there, and I’ve just interrupted.

Not really. All I was gonna say was that it was great yesterday ’cause there was Team Knight Rider, which is the, sort of, ten years later there’s a team of, uh, people with super electronic cars driving around solving crimes.
And, uh, then I flipped over and there was Buck Rogers in the 25th Century, uh, featuring, uh, Gil Gerard. D’you remember him? Good-looking fella.
And Twiki always said, “Bidi-bidi-bidi.” And, um—
No, sorry, have you— have you taken sort of, like, some real sort of heavy mixture of cocaine and [unclear]?
What’s that? “And, uh, obviously, good-looking fella, bidi-bidi,” and, uh...
[Imitates a mechanical voice] M'neh, m'neh, m'neh!
What? What are you talking about?
That's an impression of Twinkie. The little robot.
Oh, the little robot! Oh, yeah, Twiki.
The little silver robot that went “bidi-bidi-bidi”. It’s as simple as that. I’m not trying to— I’m not trying to corrupt you, I’m not trying to get, you know, confusion going.
Oh, go on, yeah. Okay, fair enough. I’ll take your word for it.
All I'm saying is, great TV shows there that we forget, you know. We're in the kitchen, Gervais, aren't we?
But everyone else has left. It's just us two.
We could go home, but somehow we're still enjoying it.
Um, and, uh, but what I was gonna talk about is, you know, there’s a lot of TV shows— there’s a lot of TV shows, Gervais, that we, we, we know and love and we remember.
But a lot of films, right, that became TV shows. MASH, obviously, the big success.
D’you know, Gervais, I read about this yesterday, fantastic. D’you know that, um, they made a TV show, right, in 1982, of Casablanca?
As Rick. What a fantastic TV show.
It'd be Casablanca, and you'd have a picture of him, wouldn't you? And every week, they'd find a different reason for him to say, play it again, Sam.
And lovely— and, yeah, and lovely Pat Coombs as, uh... as his, uh...
“Mr Rick, I’m not playing bla— backgammon for money.” “Play it again, Sam.” It’d be great. Every week, whatever it would be, I dunno what the different contrivances— it’s like a catchphrase.
Bobby Crush as the bloke on the piano. You must remember this. Oh, fantastic.
Every week he gets an excuse to play it.

Well, once, right, I was looking through, right, and there was that TV show called You Must Be the Husband, right? Yeah, it was— it was called You Must Be the Husband. And I’d never seen it before, and me and Jane were watching it, we’d just flicked over.

And we saw the last— we were gonna watch something else, and it just ended with the waiter coming up to one of ’em going, “Uh, you must be the husband.” And we thought, do they have to remember that every single week?
Deary me, that’s— that’s hard work, I tell you.
In, in TV shows. Hard work.
Oh, who played Vic— Victor Laszlo?
I don’t know anything else about it. If anyone’s ever seen it, please give me a call. What a fantastic show that would be.
Oh, I know who’d play, uh, Victor Laszlo. Um, what’s his name? Rodney. What’s his name? Nicholas Lyndhurst.
He’d be great, wouldn’t he? Nick Berry.

Nick Berry. That’d be beautiful. And I’ll tell you what it would be. It would be, uh, they’d be on a golf course, and, um, and, uh, Sam would, like, miss a stroke, wouldn’t he? And he’d just go, “Oh, play it again, Sam.”
And everyone else would laugh. It'd be beautiful.
Oh! Babybird, "If You'll Be Mine." We can keep this going forever now.
Shall we make a cup of tea?
Um, apparently, Steve, um, who says this? Uh, he doesn’t say, “Play it again, Sam.”
He says, go on, play it, Sam.

I know that, you stupid toss— oh, for goodness’ sake! I studied film for three years, for Christ’s sake, Gervais. Of course I know that! But it’s the TV show. They’re bound to have made the same mistake, aren’t they?
You can do an academic subject, then.
Of course! Oh, I can’t— oh, I’m sickened. I’m sickened. ’Cause everybody knows that, Gervais, and yet he’s come out and he’s spouting rubbish. I’m just— oh.
Um, He thinks it's a good show.
Oh, God, I'm disapp- Oh, I'm so angry!
But he likes— he likes the show.
I'm so angry, because everybody thinks I'm an imbecile.
Um, No, because I was going to mention a couple, because I came up with a couple of my own TV shows.
Have you come up with your own?
Have you talked about this in the past?
Well, yeah, yeah. Oh yeah, you know, like the, um, when they have a cliché in the title, and that’s the—
Oh, like the best one we came up with. It was fantastic.
Like a touch of frost, and it's his name.
But my favourite, this is one I came up with, right? It was called Lady of the Knight, right? But that’s “knight” spelt K-N-I-G-H-T, right?
And what is clever about it is— or, what it is, is there’s a knight, right, a knight of the realm, okay?

But it’s set about sort of, uh, 1870 or something, sort of Sherlock Holmes era, that sort of thing. And, uh, he’s a knight of the realm, you know, Lord, uh— was it Sir— Sir Johnson or whatever. And, uh, he’s a— he’s a knight, whatever.
But he doubles up as a private investigator,
And he’s got working for him a prostitute—
Right, who’s also a private investigator.
Er, and it's called Lady of the Night, you see. And it's a double—it's a double meaning, because—
'Cause she's a lady of the night, and—
She's a lady of the knight. He's a knight!

And they go round— but seriously, they go round investigating, like, crimes, sort of Whitechapel and stuff. And, um, it’s brilliant because, uh, you know, obviously she’s a prostitute or whatever and he’s a knight, and there’s a bit of sexual tension, Gervais, obviously.

And obviously got all the Victorian elements and everything. And obviously they can't associate with one another openly in the streets, because that would be, you know, he's obviously got to maintain a certain reputation.
So it’s Lady of the Knight. There’s all the intrigue and tension. What do you think about that?
That is fantastic, using all your your technical knowledge and your film study and your...
I came up with one. Go on. Starring Naughty Samantha Janus as a nun, with Diana Rigg as a mother's superior and it's called Nun the Wiser.
And the sequel, she gets pregnant and she's- she has to go and work in the kitchen, right? And that's called uh, Nun in the Oven.
I was gonna say. Yeah. Of course it is.
Of course it is. Oh, that’s beautiful, Gervais.

Remember, um, Ray Cooney, that— that thing in the eighties when all those, uh— had those farces on? And, uh, basically what he did was, um, substitute the word “life” for “wife”. He had Run for Your Wife, right? And, uh, Wife Begins at Forty.
Beautiful. Doesn't make any sense, does it, grammatically?

No. No. I- I just thought of one, like, um, I said to uh, Claire a few weeks ago that it would be like a stage play, and there'd be loads of people jumping in and out like, of hospital beds. But one- in one of the beds, one of the wives, she just wanted to die.
She’s had no quali— and it’s Whose Wife Is It Anyway? [Laughs] That’d be good, wouldn’t it?
Oh, that’d be beautiful. I love that. Touch of Frost. It’s so clever.
And the and the other one is um, uh, loads of uh, lawyers with their wives jumping in and out of bed with just underpants on, taking drugs, and it's this wife.
That's great. That's a nice touch.
Um, let's have uh, some competitions then.
But you know, I've got- I've- I've got a whole game show as well, which I could mention.
Do you want me to mention it?
Well, should we, uh, play, uh, Blue Öyster Cult? Their classic song—
I—I've got a game show, right, that I came up with.
Okay? And it features me, but I think it could be perhaps a vehicle for yourself, Gervais.
I’m gonna tell you. It’s called— basically, it’s called Ricky Gervais’ Meat Rations.
Because there's a part in there for me.
Could I play the Ricky Gervais?

It was originally called, um, it was originally called, uh... Basically, let me just summarise very briefly. I’m not gonna tell you all the games, but there is— it’s basically recreating the, uh, heady days of the war.
It's beautiful already, isn't it? It's got the nostalgia thing.
I’ve got— I’ve got a game as well.
But it’s called— it was originally gonna be called, uh, Ricky Gervais’ Fag Rations.
But apparently cigarettes weren’t rationed in the war.
So it's called Meat Rations now.
And uh, I'll tell you, some great games. My favourite is, um, oh no, what's it called? Um, to- To Be Perfectly Anne Frank.
It's a great game. It really is. It's a great game where you've got to pretend to be Anne Frank and hide from uh, sort of snooping Nazis.
It’s a great game. And there’s also, of course— well, let me go into it. There’s— there’s also, um, uh, uh, Dig for Granny.
Uh, well— or Dig for Victory, if you like. And what it means, you— you’re scavenging through rubble.
Can I just say, these— these are copyright. Anyone trying to rip me off. I mean, I’ve got the Penis Puppet Theatre.
I've got a stake in this surely haven't I?
You can have— you can have a bit of my Penis Puppet Theatre.

Yeah and I've also got a new game that I talk about after after yours. It's called Tip the Balance. And it's sort of like a game for four, and it comes it's like I'll I'll send it off to Waddington, see what you think.
I mean there's there's there's teething problems with it.
By Blue Oyster and his cult.
Yeah. And then we come back and we'll try and make some money.
Blue Öyster Cult - (Don't Fear) The Reaper
Well, you've got to be happy with that. Blue Öyster Cult, "Don't Fear the Reaper."
So go on then. So what other games are in this, uh, uh, "Ricky Gervais's Meat Rations"?
Well, it starts off... and There's the sound of an air-aids siren.
And uh, we came up with, uh... Start queuing up, Mum, for Ricky Gervais' Meat Rations.
Excellent. Do I look like, sort of, Walker out of Dad’s Army?
And, uh, what it is, the set, right, is, um, is kind of, like, half of it is an old sort of East End pub.
And the rest is kind of rubble and debris.
And a sky— a skyline of ruined, you know, uh, Britain.
And what it is, is you come in, you're fairly sort of sharp and dapper. And uh, of course, Chaz and Dave provide the music throughout the show.
And can I- ding-a-ling, ding-a-ling. And you know the dolly bird that usually comes on? She's the one with, like, uh, um, curlers, with a little, um, scarf on it.
She comes out with one of those little floral aprons.
That's it. You've got it. You've got it.
And, uh, there's a game show- there's a bit- there's a bit in the show called Roll Out the Barrel.
Uh, I don't know what happens in that.
Roll out the barrel. Oh, we could think of summat.
There's a barrel of fun sort of thing.

And there's- yeah, so there's- and there's a Dig for Victory where you've got, like, a big pile of rubble, right? And you're digging through it, scavenging for food, canned food. But if you find, like, relatives or friends-
Oh, that is fantastic. And- there must be some sort of fun with, like, gas masks.
When you can all put them on and dress up as, like, I dunno, one of the Banana Splits.
So- so that- no, every week there's the real Snork.
So it's like- it's like contestants come on, they have to think, you know, whatever, "Which one's Snork? Which one's Snork?"
So you’ve got three— maybe you’ve got three celebrities.
Yeah, [unclear] gas mask, and the real Snork.
So, you've got someone like Ted Maltzson, he pops one on. You've got Frank Bruno, yeah, and Ginny Cooper.

And they put their mask on and, like, a little outfit, and then the real Snork is there. And you’ve got to ask them questions. Like, you get— you get, like, Bernie Winters and, uh, um, Henry Cooper going, “Um, um, number three. Number three. Um, how long have you been in the Banana Splits?”

And Jilly Cooper goes, “Oh, about six years.” He goes, “Oh, I don’t know. I think the— I think the Banana Splits have been going longer than that. No, I don’t think it’s number three. Um, what— what do you think?” And, uh, Bernie Winters goes, “Mm, number one.”

“Um, uh, how did you get the job being in the Banana Splits?” And it’s probably Ted Moult or someone going, “Oh, I, um, answered an advert in the paper.” “That’s not right. They were born—” You know what I mean?
And there's Chas and Dave in the corner just going-

Yeah, “Will the real Snork...” And they all— the lights go, right, and one stands up and he sits back down again, and then the real Snork— and the others all take their masks off. And he goes, “Lovely, Jilly, what are you doing now?”
“Well, I’m, uh, I’m, uh, appearing, uh, in Puss in Boots down in, uh, Brighton.” Oh, that’d be fantastic.
I don't know, what does she do? Oh, she's a novelist.
Now appearing in Panto. I'm not letting you book the guests.
But wait a minute. I mean, I love your idea.
“Who's Snork?” It's a bit odd, isn't it, how we started off with a kind of wartime nostalgia show, but now we've sort of featured sort of quite bad seventies animal things.
Nothing wrong with the, uh, Banana Splits.
But I like that. That's a good game.
Yeah, okay, so that can be, like, a special feature, can’t it?
So I'm just going to make a note of it, because we've got Dig for Victory, uh, to be perfectly Anne Frank.
Yeah. Well, I'm full of ideas. I could probably help you on this.
Oh, this is great. Well, what other— I’m just gonna— well, maybe we’ll come up with some other ideas as we go on.
Yeah, we've still got Tip the Balance to go.
But, you know, can I just say, I did actually once try and pitch this. When I— you know when I appeared on Blockbusters?
Well, I obviously met with a producer there, and I said, I've got an idea for you.
Have we talked about this on air?
We've talked about me on Blockbusters,
But not about um, my pitching this game.

And I said to her, “Sit— sit down,” I said, “I’ve got a great idea.” And I, I tried to bill it with me as the star. She said, “Who are you?” “Steve— Steve’s— Steve’s Meat Rations.” Uh, she said, “Why are you in it?”
I said, I am, don't worry, I just, I, I'm the only one who can put it off.
And, um, she said, “Right, go on, what— what is it?” And at that time, I had none of the games.
All I had was— all I had was the title, and she went, “I like it, yeah. What are the games?” “I, um, dunno.”
If you’d have just said, “Well, I’ll stop you there, love,” and just popped a gas mask on and said, “Who am I?”
She'd have gone- she'd have gone, "Snork."
[Ricky and Steve sing the "na-na-na" tune again.]
No, it's not. Oh, we've got an ad break, then we've got a classic from Blur.
[The recording cuts to music under Ricky's voice.]
It's, uh, it's five o'clock. So, if you were gonna watch that thing that started at five to, you've missed the first five minutes of it.
So we’re doing well with this, um, new game show, aren’t we?
Yeah, we've got a few ideas there.
It’s a great idea, isn’t it? We’ve got— and we— well, we came up with a quick— another quick game, ’cause obviously so far we’ve got Dig for Victory.
Uh, To Be Perfectly Anne Frank, and, uh, Who’s Snork? Which is possibly, I think, the most popular game so far.
And also we’ve come up with a new one, haven’t we? Um, Puss in Jackboots.
Yeah. You get a beauty of the age to come out.

Yeah, maybe she comes out and she’s got a little moustache on, right, and a peaked cap pulled low and, uh, Nazi regalia. And you go— and you’ve got Bernie Winters and, uh, Ted Moult or someone, and, uh, Jilly Cooper going, “Um, so, um, you’re obviously— by the warm, warm applause, you’re— you’re much loved.”
“Yes, I am!” “Oh, thank God, um... uh, show business?” And the audience clap.
Obviously, yeah. I like that, yeah.
Um, I don't know, you—you—you're doing the, er, you're doing the, er, Nazi accent very well. Um, are you an actress? “Yes, that is correct!” Yeah. It'd be great, wouldn't it?
That’d be nice. Just do a little Nazi salute.
Yeah. A little click, That'd be lovely.
I thought of a little quick game.
And what’s that one? That’s called, um...

I thought of a quick one. It’s called, um, Get the Hell Out of Hiroshima. Right, it’s against the clock. Uh, anyway, there’s a— that’s there as well. And, uh, have we got any— any other ideas, Gervais?
It's time for the game show everyone's talking about, Make Gervais Laugh.

We've had an entry here this week, all right, and what it is, let me explain the rules. Somebody sent in a picture, Gervais, right, I'm going to show it to you now, and if you laugh, then hopefully this young fellow wins a prize.
Uh, it’s from Neil in, uh, let me see, Highgate.
Hold on, I'm laughing already, though.
Yeah, ’cause of— of the anticipation. Alright, okay.
Straighten yourself out. Now, you've not seen this picture.
Oh, it's so disappointing if it's not funny. There's nothing worse than that, you know what I mean?
Well, I think—I think you're well—
You run the risk. You run the risk.
But that’s— but that’s the nature of the game... show.
And what, what's in it for everyone else who can't see the picture or cares?
We're not here for their amusement, are we?
Alright, you know, we’re busy men. We’ve got things to do. We’ve got to entertain ourselves.
But what I would say is, what is there in this show anyway for anybody else?
At least we get a laugh.
Um, now what I would say— the other thing, though, is, is there a prize for Neil?
Yeah, if if, if I laugh. Um…
Will you give him sort of like a—a chuckle-o-meter? You know, the old—the Ricky Gervais's chuckle-o-meter.
Yeah, this is up to ten CDs.
All right then. Well, okay. 'Cause that first one we did—
—ages ago, that was, that was up to—
Right, here comes the picture. I think it looks to me like it's an internet picture.
I'll be honest with you. You ready?
Okay, here comes the picture now, Gervais.
[Paper rustles. Ricky laughs, then makes retching noises.]
Oh God. Oh God. Oh, has he done that? No.
Now, listen, what I'll do is, let's play a record, Gervais, and I will...
No, no, don't, please. Right, no. Um, when I was, uh, about sixteen, um, my nephew got, um, mumps. And all the men in my family were really worried, right?
And uh, I soon found out why. You know, obviously, if you get mumps when you're an adult, and you haven't had it before, you go sterile, or it can cause sterility.
Yeah, yeah. And, um, I was about sixteen and, uh, this worried me, and I went to my mum and I said, “Have I had mumps?” She went, “You've had one mump.”

Now, I don't know what mumps are or is, but I'm pretty sure you can't have a mump. Or, I think she meant that one side of my face swelled up, like a gobstopper, it was. But what is a mump? Or what are the mumps?
I mean, it's a viral infection, isn't it? I don't want to embarrass myself. I don't want her to be right. Like a doctor.
I don't know, can you have, like, a number of mumps or one big one big mump?
What if you had one big mump?
It's like, like a hunchback for a while? You're just like—
You're mump-backed for a while. You just walk around.
Yeah, and you don't remember... Because it's always when you're very young.
Exactly. But I had, apparently I had one mump. So I could probably— probably one of 'em, just one of 'em went a bit sterile.
Can you— so you, you can become sterile—
—if you have the mumps when you're an adult?
Can you— I mean, does that, for instance, does that— it doesn't cause, um... Say, I mean, say for instance an adult had mumps—
—and then he sort of had sex and he, and he had, and he gave birth to a child. His wife gave birth to a child.
That can't cause any other problems. It can't cause deformity or anything. It's just, no, because it's just my dad had the mumps.

I don't know. I don't know. We, we should get our facts right, really. If there's a doctor out there, I mean, can mumps cause sterility? How does it do it? I heard stories about, um, my teacher, his mate, um, had to have 'em— they swelled up and he had to put 'em in cotton wool for about a month.
'Cause they can, you know... Mumps aren't fun.
No, I'm not saying it. I mean, what— let me— all I can say, maybe, maybe you've had mumps and now you're sterile.
